name: Cua Fleet (Windows Server)

modes.label: Cua Fleet usage-based, Windows Server 2022 image
modes.note: cua.ai/pricing: CPU $0.044625/vCPU/hour, memory $0.0223125/GiB/hour; one rate for all OSes, no published Windows licence surcharge. Fleet built-in images: Ubuntu 24.04 and Windows Server 2022 only (Windows 11, macOS, Android rejected for Fleet in the SDK).

plans.name: Usage-based (dashboard run.cua.ai)
plans.note: Plan fees / free tier not on the official pricing page.

caveats: Billing granularity, minimums, storage, egress and paused-state billing are not published.
No Windows surcharge published; if one exists the estimate is low.
macOS is NOT hosted by Cua (local-only via Lume on your own Mac).
A 'Pro from $10/mo' plan appears only in third-party guides; not encoded.
Releasing a claim does not delete or scale down its pool: retained warm sandboxes can keep billing until the pool is scaled down, deleted or expires.

audit_2026_09_29.source: checked against the provider's live pricing and docs pages

snapshot_auto.quote: releasing the Fleet claim, which returns the VM to its pool and resets its disposable disk overlay
snapshot_auto.note: Fleet VMs are disposable pool replicas: release resets the disk overlay, deleting the pool removes 'its capacity and state'. The same guide: 'a replacement VM does not restore files unless you use provider storage or snapshots'. No automatic save on stop/idle documented.

snapshot_on_demand.quote: Not implemented; snapshot-derived image inputs are also rejected
snapshot_on_demand.note: Row `Sandbox.snapshot()` in the Fleet column (cua-sandbox 0.7.0/0.8.0); how-sandboxes-work also says snapshot 'is not implemented for local sandboxes or the Fleet creation paths'. Snapshot code survives only on the legacy CloudTransport (retired api.cua.ai VM API). The CLI documents `cua sb suspend` ('Suspend the sandbox, preserving memory state') but that is for local/legacy cloud; Fleet support not shown. CONFLICT: marketing homepage says 'Fork from snapshots, reproduce failures' - not backed by current docs.

harness_api.quote: The default Sandbox APIs use `computer-server` for shell, files, terminals, and screenshots.
harness_api.note: Fleet exposes computer-server (shell/files/PTY/screenshots/GUI input) and optional Cua Driver MCP; the agent loop (Cua Agent SDK, Claude Agent SDK, Codex SDK, OpenAI Agents API) runs outside or is installed by the user via recipes (Codex exec-server, Cursor worker, OpenClaw on Linux Fleet). No first-party API to start/stream/resume an in-sandbox harness.

ingress_rules.note: Only ports declared as named services on the pool template are routed through Fleet's proxy; access needs the Fleet auth lease ('A URL alone does not grant access'). Optional public signed URLs per service: 'The URL is public, time-limited, and revocable' (60 s to 24 h). No IP allowlists.

guest_firewall.note: Windows Server 2022 full VM on KubeVirt (own kernel); Windows Defender Firewall inside the guest should apply if the session has admin rights (not explicitly documented).

secret_proxy.quote: Pass task-specific credentials from the host into a sandbox at runtime.
secret_proxy.note: Secrets are passed as env vars in shell.run() commands, or via pool `claim_secrets` = claim-scoped secret delivery as files at /run/cua (Terraform pool docs). Real values enter the VM; no injecting proxy.

isolation.quote: This example creates a KubeVirt Linux pool and exposes SSH. ... runtime = "kubevirt"
isolation.note: Fleet's Windows pool uses the same runtime="kubevirt" template (firmware="efi"); KubeVirt runs guests as QEMU/KVM VMMs, matching the docs' description of Windows sandboxes booting a full VM with its own kernel from a containerDisk artifact.

image_oci.quote: The Sandbox SDK's Fleet VM template references a containerDisk artifact, with a guest disk at `/disk/disk.img`; an ordinary application container is not a substitute.
image_oci.note: Fleet does not boot arbitrary Docker/OCI application images: it requires a prebuilt raw VM disk (qcow2) wrapped as a KubeVirt containerDisk, published before pool creation. SDK image layers (apt_install/pip_install/run/copy/env) are rejected for Fleet ('Rejected' in the runtime-support table), so this is not the standard 'bring your own Docker/OCI image' capability.

anti_bot.quote: Scale Linux, Windows, macOS, and Android computer fleets for computer-use agents with one open-source MCP/CLI driver.
anti_bot.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. Cua Fleet is a computer-use VM/desktop platform (screenshot+click driver, sandboxes); no stealth/fingerprint anti-bot feature is documented anywhere in the docs or trust pages.

captcha_solving.quote: Scale Linux, Windows, macOS, and Android computer fleets for computer-use agents with one open-source MCP/CLI driver.
captcha_solving.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. No CAPTCHA-solving service is documented; Cua only ships a computer-use driver/desktop, not a browser-automation/scraping product with built-in CAPTCHA solving.

egress_ip_type.quote: The image-based `Sandbox.ephemeral()` path in `cua-sandbox` 0.7.0 accepts only the default region, `us-east-1`.
egress_ip_type.note: derived: Fleet runs on AWS-hosted KubeVirt capacity (registry at public.ecr.aws, region us-east-1). No residential/mobile egress proxying is documented anywhere, so outbound traffic is ordinary cloud-datacenter NAT egress.

volume_attach.quote: resource "fleets_pool" "windows" { name = ... cpu_cores = 4 memory = "4Gi" container_disk_image = ... runtime = "kubevirt" firmware = "efi" ... service { ... } autoscaling { ... } }
volume_attach.note: not offered: the full documented pool configuration surface (Terraform `fleets_pool` resource and the Sandbox SDK Pool/ClaimSpec) has no field for attaching an extra persistent volume/disk to a sandbox.

volume_shared.note: not offered: no shared/multi-attach volume primitive appears in the pool or claim schema; each replica boots its own containerDisk with a disposable overlay.

live_resize.quote: Use a lowercase DNS label of at most 63 characters for `name`. Changing it replaces the pool because it also owns its namespace.
live_resize.note: not offered: cpu_cores/memory are fixed pool-template fields; there is no documented API to change a running sandbox's CPU/RAM in place, only creating new replicas from a (re)applied pool spec.

own_agent_api.quote: Harnesses own the agent loop and invoke Cua Driver. Some are tied to a model provider; others let you choose the model separately.
own_agent_api.note: Cua ships a low-level driver/API (computer-server, Cua Driver MCP) to control the screen, but the task-agent loop itself is owned by third-party coding/computer-use harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, OpenAI Agents API, etc.), not a first-party Cua task agent driven via its own API.

lang_node.quote: The TypeScript Fleet SDK provides separate Node.js and browser entry points. ... You need Node.js 20 or newer.
lang_node.note: First-party TypeScript/Node.js Fleet SDK to provision, claim, and control Fleet sandboxes (create-fleet-capacity, claim-a-sandbox how-tos ship Node/TypeScript examples alongside Python).

egress_allowlist.quote: resource "fleets_pool" "windows" { name = ... cpu_cores = ... memory = ... container_disk_image = ... runtime = ... firmware = ... readiness_probe_json = ... service { ... } autoscaling { ... } }
egress_allowlist.note: not offered: the documented pool/claim configuration surface has no egress firewall, allowlist, or no-internet-mode field; outbound network policy is not mentioned anywhere in the docs.

egress_http_rules.note: not offered: only inbound named services are declared in the schema; there is no HTTP method/path-level egress rule mechanism documented.

static_egress_ip.quote: resource "fleets_pool" "windows" { name = ... cpu_cores = ... memory = ... container_disk_image = ... runtime = ... firmware = ... }
static_egress_ip.note: not offered: no fixed/static outbound IP option appears anywhere in the pool schema or docs; egress is ordinary cluster NAT.

hipaa.quote: Cua has completed its SOC 2 Type I examination. The SOC 2 Type II audit is in progress.
hipaa.note: not offered: the trust/compliance page lists only SOC 2 Type I (done) and Type II (in progress) as current status; no HIPAA/BAA program is mentioned.

sso.quote: Cua has completed its SOC 2 Type I examination. The SOC 2 Type II audit is in progress.
sso.note: not offered: no SAML/OIDC single sign-on is mentioned on the trust page, pricing page, or docs; account auth is via Clerk sign-in with no enterprise SSO option documented.

eu_data_residency.quote: The image-based `Sandbox.ephemeral()` path in `cua-sandbox` 0.7.0 accepts only the default region, `us-east-1`.
eu_data_residency.note: Fleet capacity/regions documented are US (us-east-1) only; no EU region or data-residency option is documented, consistent with the card's regions:["us"].

max_session_h.quote: Without this argument, there is no creation-age TTL from this setting.
max_session_h.note: There is no platform-imposed maximum session/claim duration; TTL (ttl_seconds_after_created) is an optional, user-set cleanup backstop on pools/claims, not a mandatory cap, so a claim can in principle run indefinitely until released or the pool is deleted.

persistent_disk.quote: releasing the Fleet claim, which returns the VM to its pool and resets its disposable disk overlay ... a replacement VM does not restore files unless you use provider storage or snapshots
persistent_disk.note: Fleet claims boot from a disposable containerDisk overlay; release/rotation resets it and no persistent volume or disk mechanism is documented (snapshots are also unimplemented). Applies equally to the Windows Server 2022 pool template.

snapshot.quote: `Sandbox.snapshot()` | Not implemented | Not implemented; snapshot-derived image inputs are also rejected
snapshot.note: Confirmed in cua-sandbox 0.8.0 docs for both local and Fleet (pool-backed) execution, including Windows Server 2022 Fleet pools. Marketing copy ('fork from snapshots') is contradicted by the versioned SDK reference.

pause_resume.quote: On Fleet, `disconnect()` drops the connection without releasing the claim. Exiting a `pool.claim()` context releases the claim, but the pool can keep warm capacity available and incur cloud usage charges.
pause_resume.note: Fleet's only claim-level lifecycle operations are bind/release/delete (and TTL-based deletion); there is no suspend-and-resume operation that preserves guest memory/CPU state for a Windows Fleet VM. The CLI's 'preserving memory state' suspend applies to local/legacy sandboxes, not Fleet.

fork.quote: `Sandbox.snapshot()` | Not implemented | Not implemented; snapshot-derived image inputs are also rejected
fork.note: Forking (cloning a running/paused sandbox) is not offered anywhere in the Fleet SDK; the only building block that could support it (snapshots) is explicitly unimplemented, and Fleet rejects snapshot-derived image inputs outright.

fork_running.quote: Not implemented; snapshot-derived image inputs are also rejected
fork_running.note: No API to fork a running Windows Fleet VM into a second live instance; only new claims from a pool's static image are possible.

memory_snapshot_fork.quote: Not implemented; snapshot-derived image inputs are also rejected
memory_snapshot_fork.note: No memory-state snapshot/fork mechanism exists for Fleet; snapshotting is unimplemented and snapshot-derived boot images are rejected.

ssh.quote: Use a distinct name for Windows. The Windows computer-server image requires UEFI, so this example sets `firmware = "efi"` and waits for the service on port `8000`. ... service { name = "computer-server" target_port = 8000 protocol = "TCP" }
ssh.note: The Windows pool template example declares only the `computer-server` service; unlike the Linux example (which explicitly declares `service { name = "ssh" target_port = 22 }`), no SSH service or sshd is documented for the Windows Server 2022 Fleet image. The only Windows+SSH doc ('Drive a Windows app over SSH') is about driving the customer's own separately-provisioned Windows machine, not Cua's Fleet VM.

wake_on_request.quote: Use a TTL as a cleanup backstop for interrupted jobs, and still release claims when work finishes. It is not an inactivity timeout or an automatic heartbeat.
wake_on_request.note: Fleet has no stop/sleep + wake-on-request model. Pools/claims only support explicit release/delete or creation-age TTL deletion; autoscaling `min_pool_size=0` removes idle warm capacity but does not resume a specific stopped machine on an incoming request.

auto_stop_idle.quote: Pools and claims accept an optional creation-age TTL. ... It is not an inactivity timeout or an automatic heartbeat.
auto_stop_idle.note: The only automatic lifecycle timer documented is a creation-age TTL (deletes regardless of activity), not an idle-based stop. No idle-detection/auto-stop feature is documented for Fleet claims or the Windows pool template.

volumes.quote: resource "fleets_pool" "windows" { name = ... cpu_cores = 4 memory = "4Gi" container_disk_image = ... runtime = "kubevirt" firmware = "efi" ... service { name = "computer-server" target_port = 8000 protocol = "TCP" } }
volumes.note: The Fleet pool schema (Terraform provider and SDK Pool/Image reference) exposes only cpu_cores, memory, the boot containerDisk image, firmware, services, and autoscaling -- no attachable extra volume/disk resource for Windows or Linux pools.

inbound_https.quote: Use a signed service URL when a person or external system needs temporary access to a service running inside a Fleet sandbox. The URL is public, time-limited, and revocable. Requests still route only to the named service on the bound sandbox.
inbound_https.note: Fleet issues public, revocable time-limited HTTPS URLs (60s-24h) to reach a named service/port inside any claimed sandbox, and unsigned authenticated HTTPS requests via `sandbox.services.request()`/`sb.services.request()` are also documented. This mechanism is generic to Fleet pools (both the Python/TS SDK and Terraform provider examples cover Linux and Windows pools identically) and is not restricted to Linux, so the Windows card's `inbound_https:false` is incorrect.

public_ipv4.quote: Requests still route only to the named service on the bound sandbox.
public_ipv4.note: All documented inbound access (service requests, signed URLs) is proxied through Fleet's own endpoint (run.cua.ai) to a named service; no Fleet doc anywhere assigns a dedicated public IPv4 address to an individual Windows (or Linux) sandbox VM.

gpu.quote: The sandbox GPU is the *Microsoft Basic Display Adapter*, which offers OpenGL 1.1. Minecraft 1.17 and later need OpenGL 3.2, so the game needs Mesa3D's `opengl32.dll` (llvmpipe), which implements OpenGL in software.
gpu.note: Explicit first-party confirmation that the Windows Fleet VM has no real/passthrough GPU: it exposes only the software Basic Display Adapter, requiring a software OpenGL implementation for 3D apps.

macos.quote: macOS | Sequoia 15 | Native macOS desktop | Local Lume VM | `ghcr.io/trycua/macos-sequoia-cua:latest` | Compatible Apple silicon host required; mutable tag; no built-in Fleet mapping.
macos.note: This card is the Windows Server 2022 Fleet product; macOS is explicitly local-only (Lume on an Apple Silicon Mac) with 'no built-in Fleet mapping', so macOS is plainly outside what this hosted Windows product offers.

arm64.quote: Windows | Server 2022; artifact architecture not established by SDK mapping | Native Windows desktop | Fleet containerDisk; local Hyper-V or QEMU | `public.ecr.aws/k5j5w0x5/cua-windows-2022:main-bac7daa3` | `Image.windows()` mapping in `cua-sandbox` 0.8.0; Fleet selects EFI.
arm64.note: Only one Windows Fleet image exists (Server 2022, EFI/x64 container disk); no ARM64 Windows build, size, or image is offered by Fleet. ARM64 appears elsewhere in the docs only for local Apple-Silicon Lume VMs (unrelated product), consistent with arm64=false for this Windows Fleet product.

private_network.quote: A service declaration gives Fleet a named route to a port in the guest. It does not install the application, start a listener, or prove that the service is ready.
private_network.note: Fleet's networking model is limited to declaring named per-port services routed through Fleet's own proxy/auth layer; no VPC, private peering, or private network between sandboxes/pools is documented anywhere in the Sandbox SDK, Terraform provider, or Fleet concept docs.

docker_inside.quote: Administrator privileges for the machine-wide package provisioning step. ... In an elevated PowerShell window
docker_inside.note: derived: the Windows Server 2022 Fleet VM is a full VM with its own kernel and confirmed Administrator/elevated-PowerShell access for installing arbitrary machine-wide software (demonstrated installing the ChatGPT desktop app + native Computer Use runtime). No doc explicitly runs Docker Desktop or Windows containers inside a Fleet Windows VM, but nothing restricts installing it given documented admin rights, matching the pattern for other full-VM Windows products.
